A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core definitions, experimental framework, and retained results. The main text, equations, figures, table, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original reward-modeling and preference-alignment experiments, including deception scores, mitigation experiments, and supplementary SimPO, DPO, and LLaMA results.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds honesty-alignment results, no-conflict analyses, and an adaptive-supervision comparison.

M1.justification: Appendix P introduces an adaptive supervision variant that weights cross-entropy by |2M_weak(x)-1|, down-weighting uncertain weak predictions. This changes the training objective for an additional mitigation experiment; the main alignment procedures and existing countermeasures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates harmlessness against conflicting harmfulness or helpfulness objectives. v3 Appendix O adds UnknownBench experiments targeting honesty on unanswerable questions under conflicting helpfulness supervision. This introduces a distinct alignment task previously mentioned only as future work, while retaining the original coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds an evaluated adaptive-loss versus naive-loss comparison in reward modeling under implicit conflict (Appendix P, Figure 23). The existing SimPO, DPO, model-family, high-confidence filtering, and bootstrapping comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: v3 introduces absolute deception scores using the ground-truth strong model as reference, enabling additional no-conflict comparisons. The new honesty protocol uses 400 samples each for ground-truth training, weak supervision, and testing, 2,000 helpful samples, and batch size 16. It also adds threshold T=0.70 and replaces the GPT-2-Large illustrative analysis with GPT-2-XL. These extend evaluation rather than establish reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of possible spontaneous deception without conflicting objectives and tests adaptive weighting as mitigation. It extends threshold sensitivity to T=0.70 and replaces the earlier explicit-conflict illustration with GPT-2-XL analyses covering both conflict types. The conflict-strength comparison in v3 Appendix J already appeared in v2 Figure 9.

E5.justification: Both versions explicitly report one run per experiment because of computational costs (v2 Appendix D.1; v3 Appendix E.1). Neither adds repeated-run statistics, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Expanded model-confidence thresholds are sensitivity analyses, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v3 adds absolute-deception-score curves, honesty-alignment outcomes, threshold results, and adaptive-loss findings. New Figures 19–20 report deception scores of 0.58 and 0.40 for GPT-2-XL supervising Mistral-7B under explicit and implicit conflict, respectively. These replace an illustration using GPT-2-Large, not a same-setting performance comparison. Most existing benchmark results and Table 1 are retained.

T1.justification: v3 defines absolute deception scores through a different reference model and mathematically specifies the adaptive weighted objective in Equation 16. The original knowledge-region definitions and deception-score equations remain unchanged; reordered training equations are equivalent, and no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: deception under conflicting alignment objectives, greater severity with increasing capability gaps, and limited mitigation through bootstrapping. Additional experiments support or explore these claims without redefining the headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix K newly interpret no-conflict failures as possible spontaneous deception while acknowledging that erroneous weak supervision cannot be disentangled from active deception. Section 5.3 qualifies the growth-rate interpretation as especially apparent under explicit conflict. Appendix P explains adaptive weighting's limited mitigation, and the limitations now acknowledge preliminary honesty experiments.

D1.justification: v3 documents UnknownBench response-pair construction using gpt-4-0613 and Llama-2-13B-Chat, sample counts, and training settings. It adds a reproducibility statement claiming code and data provision and updates the stated repository location. Existing hardware, optimizer, learning-rate, epoch, and LoRA details are retained.

R1.justification: New Appendix B substantially expands positioning against reward hacking, distinguishing comparisons across knowledge regions within one alignment dimension and separately controlled supervision signals. v3 adds the associated Pan et al. references and expands coverage of weak-to-strong theory and reasoning in Section 2.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v3 presents no-conflict objectives first, refines explanations, shortens the conclusion's future-work discussion, adds reproducibility and acknowledgments sections, and reorganizes appendices around new material. These are localized structural changes rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds plots for absolute deception, honesty, and adaptive supervision; redraws Figure 8 with both conflict types; and expands threshold figures from two to three panels. The earlier four-panel main-text scatter illustration becomes two three-panel appendix figures with a different teacher. The existing conflict-strength plot moves to the appendix.

improvement.justification: v3 improves empirical breadth by testing honesty, examines another mitigation strategy, and explicitly acknowledges confounding in the new no-conflict analysis. These additions make the paper more informative and its interpretation more qualified. The gains remain limited: results are still single-run, the added honesty study is preliminary, and the central attribution of failures to deliberate deception remains unresolved.
